articles.title: Murder-House Impostor Thriller ‘The Stand-In Family’ Wins Mirror Fiction Award at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
articles.summary: Taiwanese literary IP developer and production company Mirror Fiction announced the winners of its fifth Mirror Fiction Award and unveiled five projects for its 2027 slate at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF).
body: “This award was a clear goal for me when I created the story,” said Kong, an engineer by profession. “I had written other works before, but adapting them for the screen would have been too expensive. So this time, I started with a realistic setting and considered production costs from the beginning.”

The NT$700,000 ($22,500) Judges’ Award went to Malaysian writer Liang Xuan for “Endless Rain” (provisional title). Both winning works are eligible for publication and screen adaptation development through Mirror Fiction.

Tung Cheng-yu, CEO of Mirror Fiction, said the award was designed to encourage writers and introduce promising literary properties to potential investors. “I believe that only when you genuinely fall in love with a story can you make the best adaptation,” Tung said. “Adapting a novel for the screen is much easier than starting from scratch because the novel already has an established world,” she said.

Citing audience figures, Tung said films adapted from books drew more than 40% higher attendance than original films, while the difference for television content exceeded 60%. She did not identify the source of the figures during the presentation.

articles.title: IP Companies Spin Books Into Sold-Out Plays, Series and Signature Scents at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
articles.summary: Taiwanese companies laid out how original stories can grow from books into stage plays, series, fragrances and even travel itineraries at a Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) session on cross-sector intellectual property in Taipei.
body: Wang said the approach was partly modeled on South Korea, where IP adaptation began 30 years ago. “Policies brought in industries such as fashion and electronics to collaborate and invest in developing cultural products. That was also the origin of the Korean Wave,” she said.

IPis often starts with books, which Wang said offer a cheaper way to find stories that already have readers. A stage production can then test audience demand through ticket sales before the company moves into screen adaptations and related products.

The company’s stage play “Marital Lost Love” is based on a book by psychiatrist Deng Hui-wen. After three runs that Wang said sold out, IPis extended the project with a podcast and two fragrances tied to the production.

Its series project “Do You Still Love Me?” was developed from a novel written as the story source. The project won five awards at TCCF Pitching in 2025, more than any other project that year, including the udnFunLife IP Potential Award. Wang said the pitch worked because it told a clear, engaging story and showed how it could reach audiences and open up business opportunities.

articles.title: Sylvester Stallone Says His 20-Year Rivalry With Arnold Schwarzenegger Only Ended When He Ran for Governor and Wasn’t ‘Doing Movies Anymore’
articles.summary: Sylvester Stallone is reminiscing about his now-infamous rivalry with fellow action star Arnold Schwarzenegger through the 1980s and 1990s — and why they only laid down the hatchet when the latter ran for governor of California.
body: “So, I see this guy, and I could tell right away he’s going to be a problem,” Stallone said, referring to Schwarzenegger. “You know, we were at the Golden Globe Awards, and he’s sitting there and he’s eyeballing me, and — we call that stink eye — I said, ‘Okay, all right. I got it, pal.’ And then he wins.”

The two continued to vie for the title of top action star, with both actors liking “to challenge” one another, said Stallone. “We’re both physical, and now, who’s going to be the vanguard, the leader in that genre? So I do ‘Rambo,’ he does ‘Commando,’ and it went back and forth, back and forth, on and off screen. It was very contentious, trust me. Which I enjoyed.” The two later partnered on the movie-themed chain restaurant Planet Hollywood in 1991, but Stallone noted that they wouldn’t even get on stage together to give a speech.

articles.title: AI Could Make Filmmaking Costlier Than the 35mm Era, Korean Pioneers Warn at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
articles.summary: AI is already slashing the cost of commercials, but runaway token fees and piecemeal revisions could leave feature producers paying more than in the days of 35mm film, a Korean AI production pioneer told Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.
body: Studio Meta-K’s Kim Kwang-jib and MBC C&I’s Lee Sang-wook unpacked costs, hybrid shoots and new crew roles as Lee’s AI feature ‘Raphael’ heads to Korean cinemas.
“If they raise token costs roughly tenfold, it could go above what the films we’re shooting now cost,” Kim said. “KRW500 million could become KRW5 billion ($3.66 million).”

Hollywood, with KRW200 billion ($146.6 million) budgets, could absorb that and still make very cheap AI films, Kim said. Korean, Taiwanese and other Asian features typically shoot live action and VFX for KRW3 billion-KRW5 billion ($2.2 million-$3.66 million), and a tenfold jump would force them to ask whether AI is efficient at all.

articles.title: Hollywood banks on Ebenezer to bring Johnny Depp in from the cold
articles.summary: Dickens character is actor’s first big studio role after years overshadowed by legal battles with ex-wife Amber Heard. “It’s good to be back,” Johnny Depp declares in the trailer for Ebenezer, in which he stars as Charles Dickens’s miserly Scrooge – his first big Hollywood studio production in…
body: The message is clear: this is Depp’s comeback, after years in which his career was overshadowed by legal battles with his former wife Amber Heard.

Paramount has made a point of invoking Depp’s most famous roles – the trailer opens with references to Captain Jack Sparrow, Edward Scissorhands and the Mad Hatter, before announcing: “The master of misfits returns.”
When the film opens on 13 November, it will be a test – not just of whether Depp can still sell cinema tickets, but whether Hollywood can restore him to the ranks of mainstream leading men.
“I think Ebenezer will serve as a bellwether for the industry as to Depp’s bankability,” said Robert Mitchell, the director of theatrical insights at Gower Street Analytics.

articles.title: ‘Life is like a heartbeat. It’s up and down, up and down’: Michelle Yeoh on casting cliches, marriage at 60 and playing a robot in Blade Runner 2099
articles.summary: Ballet dancer, action hero, Bond girl... The actor won an Oscar for Everything Everywhere All At Once but she’s been through some challenges on the way. Before agreeing to appear in Blade Runner 2099, Michelle Yeoh received a letter – “an amazing letter, a love letter” – from Silka Luisa, the…
body: Yeoh is an actor who likes to figure things out for herself and, in the prep stages for Blade Runner 2099, the key question she thought about while building her character was, “What is it to be human? Are you born with humanity or does it come from the things you go through?”

As fans of Yeoh will know, however, the actor started out as a dancer, moved to martial arts movies in the 80s and is as robustly physical as any in Hollywood. An action star at heart, Yeoh is quick on her feet and unprecious in her outlook – so much so that, on occasion, she has found Hollywood a bit cautious compared with the wild west of the Hong Kong film industry she came up in as a young woman. “I’m tiny, I’m petite, five foot four,” she says, yet her ability to change her affect through movement is so intense, so persuasive, that, placed alongside Hunter Schafer, her much taller co-star in Blade Runner, “somehow you feel I loom over her”.

articles.title: Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why “Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians”
articles.summary: As Camerimage turns 34, its director explains how the world's leading festival on the art of cinematography continues to embrace new technology while drawing the line on fully AI-generated films.
body: Camerimage, the world’s premier festival devoted to the art of cinematography, turns 34 this year, and it arrives in Torun, Poland, Nov. 7-14, with its founder in both a combative and reflective mood.

Joe Walker, the editor behind Dune and 12 Years a Slave, is also being feted and will chair the Main Competition jury, while Polish cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, whose Disclosure Day is screening in contention, receives THR ’s Visionary award.
Speaking to THR ahead of this year’s fest, Zydowicz said Camerimage will remain open to a “diversity of techniques and technologies” but draws the line at fully AI-generated films.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Zydowicz spoke about the festival’s growing ambitions, the reason why Poland seems to produce so many great cinematographers, and why the human eye will never be replaced.

articles.title: All 4 Cillian Murphy Performances In Christopher Nolan Movies, Ranked
articles.summary: Cillian Murphy has played Batman villains, real-life scientists, and more in Christopher Nolan's films. Let's rank his performances in the director's work.
body: Like many filmmakers, Christopher Nolan often works with the same actors across different projects. Sir Michael Caine has appeared in eight Nolan films total. In second place, with room to eventually become no. 1 given Caine's retirement, is Cillian Murphy.

Murphy has acted in six films directed by Nolan, in chronological order: "Batman Begins," "The Dark Knight," "Inception," "The Dark Knight Rises," "Dunkirk," and their shared magnum opus "Oppenheimer." This prosperous creative relationship all started when Murphy auditioned to play Bruce Wayne in "Batman Begins." The two recall that they both knew Murphy wasn't the right pick for the Dark Knight, but Murphy's acting impressed Nolan enough that he fought, and won, to cast Murphy instead as one of the movie's villains: Doctor Jonathan Crane, the Scarecrow.

articles.title: Knicks defend Taylor Swift after players name her 'fakest celebrity fan'
articles.summary: The pop superstar's appearances at NBA games were deemed "a little performative" by New York Knicks point guards Tyler Kolek and Miles McBride.
body: The New York Knicks has defended superstar Taylor Swift, after players named her as the fakest celebrity fan.
"At the Knicks games, I would say it's very performative, cause like they just want to be seen at the game, they're not necessarily fans. Maybe Taylor Swift?" Kolek responded.
In May and June this year, Swift attended Game Three of the NBA Eastern Conference Finals in Cleveland and Game Four of the NBA Finals in New York City.
"I don't know if I've seen her at any other games," Kolak said.

articles.title: Sarah Michelle Gellar Passed On A Martin Scorsese Movie Because Of Buffy The Vampire Slayer
articles.summary: Martin Scorsese and Sarah Michelle Gellar would've worked together on this film if Gellar's commitments to Buffy the Vampire Slayer hadn't prevented it.
body: Martin Scorsese's filmography is filled with films that took decades to get off the ground. By the 21st Century, Scorsese had settled into a statesman of cinema stature, and (to the joy of cinephiles everywhere) he's cashed in decades of chits and clout to deliver passion projects like 2016's "Silence," 2019's "The Irishman," and 2002's "Gangs of New York."

The latter draws on a 1928 nonfiction book, "The Gangs of New York" by Herbert Ashbury, that tracked the history of New York's organized crime from the 19th to 20th Century. As the book and movie show, that tale is intertwined with how Irish and Italian immigrants settled in New York went from spat-upon outsiders to true Americans.

articles.title: Gene Roddenberry Wrote An Unmade Pilot For A Non-Sci-Fi Show About A Classic Hero
articles.summary: As Star Trek: The Original Series was still airing, creator Gene Roddenberry wrote a pilot script about a classic non-sci-fi hero - but it was never made.
body: In David Alexander's book "Star Trek Creator: The Authorized Biography of Gene Roddenberry," it was revealed that back in 1967, Roddenberry wrote a pilot episode for a Robin Hood TV series called — what else? — "Robin Hood."

Little is known about his "Robin Hood" pilot, although Alexander's biography does contain a letter that Roddenberry wrote to "a friend" about the script he was working on. Roddenberry wanted to make a revisionist version of Robin Hood, adding a modern edge to the character. He wanted to rid Robin Hood of his traditional corniness and fresh-faced heroism, as one might see in Michael Curtiz's legendary 1938 feature film "The Adventures of Robin Hood." Several decades after Curtiz's movie, Roddenberry wanted to make an updated Robin Hood wherein he was meant to be something of an antihero.
The writer was seemingly taking the "dark and gritty" path, decades before that became trendy in Hollywood. As for things like casting, direction, and individual stories, we can only speculate.
